summary.title: Town Meeting rejects Forest Ridge taking, funds special education reserve in full
summary.dek: Members also halve retiree health payment and approve seven of eight preservation projects before adjourning at 10:44 p.m.
summary.body:
Winchester’s Fall Town Meeting rejected the proposed eminent domain taking of Forest Ridge on Monday night, put the full $400,000 into the schools’ special education reserve and cut a payment to the town’s retiree health trust in half. Members decided five articles before adjourning at 10:44 p.m. They resume at 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12, at Winchester High School.

## What members decided
• Forest Ridge: Article 26 failed on a clicker vote at about 10:12 p.m., 36 yes, 122 no and one abstention, far short of the two-thirds needed. The Conservation Commission proposed the taking of the parcel off Forest Circle, and Commission Chair Tracy Olson said delay risks up to $1.7 million in grants and earmarks. Late in the debate, Select Board Chair Anthea Brady read a letter from Bell Point LLC, which has an agreement to buy the land, urging the town to drop eminent domain and pursue a voluntary deal. She said the letter described an earlier Bell Point project in Essex, not a firm offer for Forest Ridge. The Select Board split 2-2 on the article, and the Finance Committee recommended unfavorable action. In May, Town Meeting rejected a voluntary $3 million purchase of the land, 105-59.
• Special education reserve: Article 29 passed in full on a voice vote after members rejected an amendment to cut it to $200,000. The School Committee chair said the reserve held $3,780.55 as of Sept. 30, down from a peak of about $413,000.
• Retiree health: Members approved Select Board member Michelle Prior’s amendment to Article 19, 98-46, cutting the free cash transfer to the town’s other post-employment benefits trust from $350,000 to $175,000. The amended article then passed unanimously.
• Personnel: Article 24 passed unanimously. It ratifies a new police superiors contract and creates a budget director position.
• Community preservation: Seven of eight Article 25 projects passed, totaling $870,500. The $50,000 Nutile Field master plan failed 65-93 after members said the town should plan all its fields together.

## Earlier in the evening
The session opened with a standing ovation for Allan Rogers and John Suhrbier, who are retiring from the Housing Partnership Board after 70 years of combined service. Before the meeting, the Select Board deadlocked on Forest Ridge and on the retiree health transfer and voted 3-1 to back making the Committee on Names a standing Town Meeting committee.

## What comes Thursday
Still to come are Articles 30 and 33 through 45. They include a study of the Sanborn Carriage House, the sidewalk snow removal bylaw, the Committee on Names, five citizen petitions and a fiscal 2027 tax levy reduction. Nov. 16 is held in reserve if members need a fourth night.

summary.title: Town Meeting approves $4.8 million in capital projects and three zoning changes
summary.dek: Members adjourn at 10:30 p.m. with Forest Ridge, a $350,000 retiree health transfer and the schools’ special education reserve still ahead
summary.body:
Winchester’s Fall Town Meeting approved about $4.8 million in capital projects, three zoning bylaw changes and a slate of routine articles Thursday night, then adjourned at 10:30 p.m. with its most contested questions still ahead. Members resume at 7 p.m. Monday, Nov. 9, at Winchester High School.

## What members decided
• Capital spending: Members passed all six capital articles, 10 through 15, mostly by unanimous voice vote. They approved $1.73 million for four vehicles, including a $1.1 million replacement for Fire Engine 4; $720,000 for roads, sidewalks and traffic calming; $410,000 to design fixes for Ambrose School’s failing heating system, aging building controls and hot classrooms at two other schools; $170,000 for design work at the high school, Lincoln and Mystic; $840,000 for a new columbarium and two water projects; and $900,000 to rebuild Lincoln School’s walkways and stairs, paid partly with leftover Muraco bond money. Two traffic motions and the columbarium carried with two-thirds majorities rather than unanimously.
• Zoning: The Planning Board’s three articles passed. They let owners of narrow lots build conforming additions by right, lower the minimum lot width in the RDA district from 120 feet to 100, eliminate the downtown review subcommittee and trim Zoning Board of Appeals paperwork. The lot-width article drew a two-thirds majority, not unanimity.
• Routine business: Twelve consent agenda articles passed together, including a $10 dog license fee increase, a school transportation revolving fund and the return of $1.15 million in unused Muraco borrowing authority. Article 3 was indefinitely postponed. Members also received the town reports, the Planning Board report and the Capital Planning report, and paid $33,032 in prior-year bills.

## What remains unresolved
• Article 19: The moderator pulled this $350,000 free cash transfer toward retiree health costs from the consent agenda. The Select Board took no position Nov. 2, when a motion for a favorable recommendation died for lack of a second.
• Article 26, Forest Ridge: The Conservation Commission wants authority to take about 13.4 acres by eminent domain, which needs a two-thirds vote. The Select Board put off its recommendation until its meeting Thursday before Town Meeting, and Winchester News has not confirmed whether it took a position. Even a yes vote only authorizes a taking; the board would have to vote separately to carry it out.
• Spending questions: The schools’ $400,000 special education reserve (Article 29), a $50,000 Carriage House study the Select Board opposes (Article 30) and $331,466 for permitting and budget software (Article 33) are all still ahead.
• The budget behind them: The Long Range Financial Planning Committee put next year’s deficit at more than $6 million. The Finance Committee warned that the town leans too heavily on free cash. School Committee Chair Timothy Matthews said an operating override is urgently needed.

## What comes Monday
Members still have to act on Articles 19, 24 through 26, 29, 30 and 33 through 45. That includes five citizen petitions, Articles 39 through 43, and two articles, 44 and 45, for which no motion had been printed. Select Board Chair Anthea Brady has said she expects Article 26 on the second or third night, Nov. 9 or 12. Nov. 12 is also scheduled, and Nov. 16 is held in reserve.

The warrant tracker has the status of every article.

updates.title: Schools make case for $50,000 Sanborn Carriage House study
updates.dek: Bellaire says town has wrestled with vacant building over three decades; Select Board and Finance Committee oppose request
updates.body:
School Committee member John Bellaire of Precinct 2 presented Article 30, which asks for $50,000 to hire a consultant to study refurbishing, replacing or demolishing the Sanborn Carriage House. The money would combine $19,000 left over from earlier carriage house efforts with $31,000 in free cash. The study itself would not choose an option.

## Where the boards stand
• Select Board: Unanimous unfavorable action. Chair Anthea Brady said the main concern was using free cash for the study.
• Finance Committee: Unanimous unfavorable action. Chair Kathryn Hughes cited Town Meeting’s spring vote, which left the historical society room to pursue other funding, and said the study is not a good use of free cash now.
• Historical Commission: Unanimous support, subject to reasonable costs. Michelle McCarthy of Precinct 7 said the Commission supports adaptive reuse and preservation of the building.

[[inline:1]]

## The building
Bellaire said the carriage house is a two-story building of roughly 3,000 square feet from the early 20th century, at 15 High St. It sits between Ambrose School and the Sanborn House and is under the School Committee’s control. It has been empty since 1994, and the town pays about $3,000 a year to insure it. A 2004 estimate put renovation at $873,000.

“Whether you want to see it knocked down and paved over, or whether you want to see it saved, none of us, I would contend, are happy with the current state of the building,” Bellaire said.

## How it got here
Town Meeting overwhelmingly rejected a $5.9 million plan to move the schools’ central office into the building. This spring, it rejected a School Committee and Select Board article to demolish it. Over the summer, the School Committee declined to back a Winchester Historical Society application to the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation for roof repairs. As of Nov. 2, the Society reports verbal interest in donations of $200,000 to $300,000, Bellaire said.

Debate is under way.

updates.title: Town Meeting honors 100-year-old parade leader, retiring detective and longtime capital planner
updates.dek: Lipper-Garabedian, elected to state Senate, pledges open door as third session opens with 129 of 192 members present
updates.body:
Town Meeting opened its third session at 7:07 p.m. Thursday at Winchester High School. By 7:09 p.m., 129 of the 192 members had checked in.

State Rep. Kate Lipper-Garabedian, who was elected Nov. 3 to the 5th Middlesex state Senate seat, told members she will keep an open-door policy when she takes office Jan. 6. “As a former city councilor in Melrose, I know how important the local-state partnerships really are,” she said.

Moderator Philip Frattaroli then led three recognitions, each met with a standing ovation:
• Margie Labedz, 100, who Frattaroli said has run the Veterans Day parade and the Veterans of Foreign Wars lodge for almost 50 years.
• Detective Steven Fields, who is retiring from the Winchester Police Department after 44 years. He began as a patrol officer in 1983 and served on the department’s honor guard and motorcycle unit. He also served on the Northeast Law Enforcement Council’s mountain bike unit, working presidential inaugurations, Boston Marathons and Red Sox World Series games, Frattaroli said. “I have been told that Detective Fields has issued over 10,000 traffic tickets. In his distinguished career, it’s unclear how many of those were town meeting members,” Frattaroli said.
• Helen Philliou of Precinct 5, who is stepping down after 40 years in Town Meeting. She served more than 20 years on the Capital Planning Committee, more than a decade as chair. Frattaroli credited her with bringing institutional knowledge and historical perspective to the Committee.

Frattaroli showed a football graphic placing Town Meeting at the 32-yard line of the warrant and said members might still finish in three nights with some cooperation.

updates.title: Third night of Town Meeting takes up Carriage House, snow rules and citizen petitions
updates.dek: Members return with 14 articles left after rejecting Forest Ridge eminent domain Monday; Nov. 16 is held in reserve.
updates.body:
Town Meeting resumes at 7 p.m. at Winchester High School for its third session, with 14 of the 45 articles left: 30 and 33 through 45. Monday, Nov. 16, is held in reserve if members need a fourth night.

• Sanborn Carriage House (Article 30): The School Committee wants $50,000 in free cash to study refurbishing, replacing or demolishing the building. The study would not itself choose an option. The Select Board voted 4-0 against it.
• Software (Article 33): Two motions totaling $331,465.68. One would use $233,359.39 left in old free cash project accounts for permitting and licensing software; the other would spend $98,106.29, including $92,493.71 in new free cash, on budget software. The Select Board deferred a position Nov. 2.
• Sidewalk snow removal (Article 34): The Disability Access Commission’s bylaw would require at least 36 inches of cleared sidewalk and clear curb ramps, with fines of $25, $50 and $75.
• Land items (Articles 35 through 37): A small parcel tied to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority station, easements for the Waterfield housing project and acceptance of about 16 acres of conservation land under the Montvale Land settlement. Each needs two-thirds, and the Select Board backs all three.
• Committee on Names (Article 38): It would become a standing Town Meeting committee with seven voting members. The Select Board voted 3-1 Monday to recommend it.
• Citizen petitions (Articles 39 through 43): Rezonings at 114 Church St. and 18 Raymond Place, two Ledges articles that would create one new house lot and a call for separate ballot votes on unrelated parts of future overrides.
• Tax levy (Article 44): The warrant allows available funds to reduce the fiscal 2027 levy. No amount had been printed in the motion book.

Monday, members rejected the Forest Ridge eminent domain taking, 36-122, and put the full $400,000 into the schools’ special education reserve. Summaries, video and posts from the first two nights follow tonight’s posts.

updates.title: Town Meeting funds special education reserve at $400,000, rejects cut to $200,000
updates.dek: Voice votes defeat amendment and earlier call for closing debate; Brady and Cooney warn of reductions
updates.body:
Town Meeting put $400,000 into the special education reserve Monday, passing Article 29 in full on a voice vote. Members first rejected an earlier motion to end debate, which needed two-thirds, and an amendment to cut the amount to $200,000, both on voice votes. The School Committee sponsored the article, which replenishes a reserve the district drained last spring.
• Shamus Brady of Precinct 1, who works as a special education director, warned that the state is cutting circuit breaker aid, which helps districts pay for high-cost special education students, in many districts. Unexpected placements do happen, he said, and he urged members to vote no on the cut.
• Norah Cooney of Precinct 5 said teachers are telling her the school cuts mean special education students are not being served properly, including her own daughter. She urged members to support what the School Committee asked for.
• Pamela Cort of Precinct 5 asked whether unspent reserve money counts toward the town’s reserves when its bond rating is reviewed. The answer was yes.
The Select Board voted 3-1 Nov. 2 to recommend favorable action on the article, with Michelle Prior voting no because she favored $200,000.

updates.title: Town Meeting rejects Forest Ridge taking 36-122
updates.dek: Measure falls far short of two-thirds, so Select Board lacks authority to take land

image.credit: WINCHESTER NEWS STAFF PHOTO / WILL DOWD

updates.body:
Town Meeting rejected Article 26 on a clicker vote Monday, 36 yes, 122 no and one abstention, falling far short of the two-thirds needed to authorize the Select Board to take Forest Ridge by eminent domain. The Conservation Commission had proposed the taking of the parcel off Forest Circle.

Under Town Counsel Karis North’s Nov. 3 memo, no taking can happen without a two-thirds Town Meeting vote and a Select Board majority, so the Board has no authority to take the land. The vote follows Town Meeting’s May rejection of a voluntary $3 million purchase, 105-59.

## Where the boards stood
• Select Board: Split 2-2, with no recommendation.
• Finance Committee: Unfavorable action, with one member dissenting.
• Winchester Committee on Community Preservation: Conditional support for conserving the land, with limits on funding.
• Housing Partnership Board: Voted 7-3 to recommend that Town Meeting delay.

## What happens next
Commission Chair Tracy Olson said earlier that delay risks up to $1.7 million in grants and earmarks. The materials did not say what happens to that money now. Bell Point LLC, which has an agreement to buy the land, has not said what it plans next.

updates.title: Brady reads Bell Point letter urging Town Meeting to drop eminent domain authority
updates.dek: Bettencourt says he saw it only weeks ago; Cort cites unmet needs in schools and municipal buildings
updates.body:
Debate on Article 26 has ended and members are voting. In the last stretch, Select Board Chair Anthea Brady read from a letter Bell Point LLC sent the Board and the Finance Committee, Select Board member Michael Bettencourt said he saw it only weeks ago, and Pamela Cort of Precinct 5 urged members to vote no.

## The Bell Point letter
A member asked whether the buyer has offered to put acres into deed-restricted conservation, and why the town would take by eminent domain something it is being offered.
Brady said the buyer’s letter described earlier work and asked the Board and the Finance Committee to evaluate whether local controls, including the Residential Cluster Development Overlay District, could avoid eminent domain. She said the buyer described an earlier project in Essex, on a property of about 85 acres, where more than 50 acres were permanently preserved. The buyer has not offered to do that here, she said. It has said it has a history of doing so.
Later, with the language in hand, Brady read the letter’s request: that the Board and the Finance Committee recommend amending the article to remove eminent domain authority while preserving the town’s ability to pursue a voluntary acquisition or conservation agreement.

## Bettencourt: ‘withheld from us’
Bettencourt said the developer does not own the land and has no legal authority to make promises. He said “this letter from the developer was withheld from us,” that he received it only a couple of weeks ago, and that leadership decided not to provide it earlier. He said he takes the developer at its word that it would work with the town if it ever buys the land, and the town would be interested in a project with an owner who gets control.
It is more beneficial to the town to buy and preserve the land, he said. He said it is unlikely to be developed soon, but its value in Winchester makes development a growing prospect.

## Cort: ‘harm is occurring now’
Frattaroli reminded members that high school students were waiting for the decision.
Cort said she would love to see the land conserved but sees too many open questions and risks. She said she asked herself whether she would take on this risk for her own family, and her answer is no. She said she campaigned for an override with a promise to spend the town’s money responsibly, and does not see authorizing the taking as responsible.
She agreed that Washington and Swanton streets is a success, with a building going up, but said it cost the town more than it knew. She voted to postpone that project indefinitely because it was premature, she said, and was told environmental remediation was not necessary.
Development of Forest Ridge before spring is not a realistic prospect, Cort said, and she asked why members would authorize eminent domain. She said losing federal funds would be a real harm, as would development. A worse harm, she said, is tying up money the town needs for clean air in Town Hall for municipal employees and for a reasonable math curriculum. “Students are getting harmed right now,” she said.

## The last speaker
Carol Savage of Precinct 5, the last speaker the moderator took, said she agreed with earlier comments about how the decision could affect past and future overrides. She said she wished members had a crystal ball when they voted last spring.

updates.title: Town counsel says town owes minimum payment at taking even if borrowing fails; Prior cites Wright-Locke debt
updates.dek: Cooney warns of schools’ needs and spring override uncertainty in Article 26 debate

inlineImages.alt: A woman in a white striped sweater holds a phone and speaks into a microphone at a balcony railing.
inlineImages.caption: Norah Cooney of Precinct 5 speaks on Article 26 at Town Meeting Monday.
inlineImages.credit: WINCHESTER NEWS STAFF PHOTO / WILL DOWD

updates.body:
Town counsel told Town Meeting that the town would owe the owner a minimum payment the moment the Select Board takes Forest Ridge, even if members have not approved the borrowing. Select Board member Michelle Prior urged a yes vote, citing the town’s debt on Wright-Locke Farm, and Norah Cooney of Precinct 5 warned about the town’s school needs.

## Who pays if borrowing fails?
Mark Feblowitz of Precinct 1 asked which body approves the borrowing, whether the Board could take the land before that approval and what happens if Town Meeting rejects the borrowing.
Town Counsel Karis North said the authorization has to come from Town Meeting. If the Board takes the property and Town Meeting does not authorize the borrowing, she said, the town is still responsible. Eminent domain law requires it to offer the initial payment, known as the pro tanto amount, when the Board executes the order of taking and records it at the registry.
North said she would expect the Board not to execute the order until funding is authorized, because the town would owe at least the pro tanto amount, and more if it is challenged. A judgment against the town would have to be paid from whatever funds are available, she said, and the general laws offer several ways to do that.
Feblowitz said he strongly supports the environmental case but strongly opposes the “aspirational description” that follows the motion. He said he does not expect it to play out as planned, and that a fiscally moderate-to-conservative town should not rely on an aspirational plan to pay for it.

## Prior: a funding source exists
Prior said she wanted to explain why she supported a favorable recommendation, since a Board member who opposed it had spoken.
• Funding: The Winchester Committee on Community Preservation has voted conditional support, as Christina Marshall read earlier. The Committee’s membership could change, Prior said, but it supports the article now.
• Outside counsel: Prior said McGonigle told members the Board was informed that town counsel does not defend eminent domain cases. She did not know that until it came up, she said, but the town hires outside counsel for labor and other issues and would do so here. “So be it,” she said.
• Wright-Locke Farm: Responding to an earlier speaker, Prior said the town was left with a $3.4 million balance after the land trust raised more than $8 million. The town still pays debt service on it from the operating budget, $226,000 this year, and will until 2035. There was no community preservation money then, she said. Now there is a dedicated source that does not touch the operating budget or the capital stabilization funds.
“I think we ought to support this article,” Prior said.

## Cooney: ‘incredibly irresponsible’
[[inline:1]]
Cooney, at her first fall Town Meeting, said conservation is an important town value but that members’ primary role includes the town’s fiscal health. “The financial risks here seem incredibly irresponsible,” she said.
She noted that voters rejected an override in the spring, that no one knows whether another will be on the spring ballot, and that the Select Board has not given a clear indication. Members should know that before voting, she said.
The School Committee said its budget next year depends on an override that may or may not come, Cooney said. She said teachers lack support, special education needs are unmet and the schools have no math curriculum. Many outstanding capital needs also rely on community preservation money, she said, and tying that money up could pull from the free cash the schools will need.

updates.title: Bettencourt cites ‘very low risk’ of lawsuit over Forest Ridge as others urge waiting
updates.dek: Sullivan points to Nahant case; assessor confirms $4.9 million valuation while debate continues

image.alt: A bearded man in glasses and a dark jacket speaks at a podium microphone beside an American flag while Town Meeting members sit in the foreground.
image.caption: Select Board member Michael Bettencourt speaks on Article 26 at Town Meeting Monday.
image.credit: WINCHESTER NEWS STAFF PHOTO / WILL DOWD

updates.body:
Town Meeting members kept debating Article 26 on the floor. Select Board member Michael Bettencourt defended the taking as low risk, while other members urged the town to wait until Bell Point buys the land.

## Ending debate
Brian Vernaglia of Precinct 4 asked whether a vote to end debate needs a majority or two-thirds. Moderator Philip Frattaroli said two-thirds. A yes vote would end debate and send members straight to the vote on the article, he said.

## A question: how can it go right?
Michelle Bergstrom of Precinct 3 said she served on the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation when Forest Ridge first came before it. The Committee pressed the proponents to find other money, she said, and they came back with state grants. She said she is not sure any project has drawn more scrutiny. After a long discussion of what could go wrong, she asked the proponents to explain how eminent domain can go right.

## Bettencourt: ‘very low risk’
Bettencourt said the Select Board has pursued Forest Ridge since 2021 and has spent thousands of dollars on legal work and appraisals. “Eminent domain is never our first option,” he said.
• The model: He pointed to the Swanton and Washington streets taking, where the town was also told to expect a lawsuit. The town did its homework, he said, and the appraisals are what count in court. It first asked Town Meeting for $3 million, then explained why the price was $5 million, while the owners said it was worth $8 million. The appeals period has passed, he said, and the former owner can no longer challenge it.
• The counsel: The Select Board hired eminent domain counsel, Rich Bowman, who advised on the Swanton and Washington streets taking, Bettencourt said. He said that counsel sees “very low risk of litigation” here, and that neither town counsel nor McGonigle claims to be an expert in eminent domain.
• The risk of waiting: The real danger, he said, is losing federal and state money for land that will not come available again.
• Bell Point: Bell Point did not buy the land outright, so a taking and any lawsuit would be with the property’s owners, not the developer. Developers do not buy outright, he said, because they can go bankrupt when permits fail, as happened at Converse Place.
He said the town can do both: more affordable housing in the town center and conservation here, as with Wright-Locke Farm.

## Sullivan: wait for Bell Point
Maura Sullivan of Precinct 1 said she wants the land kept undeveloped forever but is not comfortable acquiring it by eminent domain. “We could lose even if we win by locking ourselves into a price that we cannot afford,” she said.
• The Nahant example: She said the town of Nahant took land from Northeastern University for a marine science center expansion, and the university challenged it. After an eight-year fight that reached the Supreme Judicial Court, Nahant prevailed, she said, but it paid for years of litigation and now owes whatever the court finds is fair market value. Nahant estimated $2.2 million, she said, and Northeastern believes it is closer to $6 million.
• The agreement: The Select Board tried to negotiate with the owner more than a year ago, she said, and members have not seen the agreement between the owner and Bell Point or its terms. She said it would be more prudent to wait until Bell Point buys the land, so the town would know what was paid and whether the Conservation Commission’s appraisal was too high or too low.
• The exposure: If the appraisal is too high, she said, the town overpays. If it is too low, the taking could be challenged, as the buyer has said it might be, and the town could owe more plus legal fees. “I don’t know where that money would come from,” she said.

## Appraisals and the assessor
A Precinct 5 member said the assessor’s database appeared to show the parcel assessed at $3.275 million. Frattaroli called on the town assessor, who said the figure is $4.9 million. The member noted that the owners pay taxes on a $4.9 million value, and asked how well it would go in court for the town to say the land is worth $2.85 million when it takes it.

Vernaglia recalled that the Washington and Swanton streets parcel was appraised at $3.15 million in fall 2020 by T.H. Reenstierna, the firm that valued Forest Ridge at $3.27 million in February. A year later, he said, the firm put the Washington and Swanton streets value at $5.3 million, or $2.15 million more, and the town is now trying to sell it for $4 million.
[[inline:1]]
“It’s not been a success; it’s been a failure,” he said of the town’s eminent domain experience. He said he would love to preserve the land and asked the Select Board to negotiate a price and return with it.

## How long would a yes last?
Vernaglia asked Town Counsel Karis North how long a yes vote would remain active. North said no set limit exists, and neither case law nor statute addresses it. It is generally thought, she said, that an authorization not used within a couple of years goes stale and would have to return to Town Meeting. Frattaroli said follow-up questions would be limited, and reminded members that 16 articles remain.

## ‘Wait for the spring’
A member who referred to joining the Select Board after an earlier 40B proposal said most of the land is unbuildable and no one has proposed to build or to buy it. The question tonight is not conservation or development, he said, but whether to write a blank check for more than $4.9 million plus legal fees. If a developer buys it by spring, he said, the town will know the value, and no tree will come down before then. He said he considered moving to postpone indefinitely but would not, and favors waiting.

updates.title: McGonigle calls Forest Ridge taking a ‘blank check’; public works director sees little drinking water risk
updates.dek: Floor debate pits conservation values against lawsuit exposure as Bell Point’s $5 million valuation looms
updates.body:
Town Meeting members and a Select Board member debated Article 26 on the floor, weighing the value of conserving Forest Ridge against the financial and legal risk of an eminent domain taking. Select Board member Bill McGonigle, who voted against recommending the article, called it “a blank check.”

## Questions about the risk
Amy Beliveau of Precinct 7 said members are not debating whether the land should be conserved or developed, or any project, but whether to authorize the Select Board to take it by eminent domain. She asked the Select Board members who voted no to explain their risk factors.

## McGonigle: “a blank check”
McGonigle said he sees the article as a blank check that a jury would fill in, probably three to five years from now.
• The challenge: Bell Point told the Board during public comment that it intends to challenge the valuation of any taking, McGonigle said, and he takes that as a credible threat. He said he spent two years at a boutique law firm handling takings and more recently helped defend the town against a taking lawsuit.
• The money: The town would deposit $2.85 million with the court and could not touch it once the owner challenges, he said. Bell Point has said it can present a valuation close to $5 million. He expects a trial of at least three years, with a jury likely landing somewhere in the middle. The town would then owe the difference, statutory interest, which he put at 12%, and legal fees. The materials did not include the award amount needed to turn that rate into dollars.
• The lawyers: Town counsel has said she is not prepared to defend a taking, McGonigle said, so the town would have to hire outside eminent domain counsel at higher rates. He called it a potential “budget buster.”
• The grant: A challenge would cost the town the $1 million federal grant “for sure,” he said, making the price $1 million higher right away.
• The budget: He pointed to town finances, saying the town lacks a math curriculum and is struggling to keep up repairs and fund retiree benefits.
• The land: McGonigle said the land would be conserved by default, because two attempts to develop it in the 2010s failed and the assessor’s estimate is that it can support perhaps one single-family house. Any development would need to clear the Planning Board, the Zoning Board and the Conservation Commission, he said.
• Taxes and upkeep: The land now yields about $50,000 a year in taxes, he said. The Department of Public Works director told him the town would have to maintain the property, including perimeter trees that could fall onto neighbors.

“Once we take it, we can’t go back, and that’s just not a risk that I’m willing to take,” McGonigle said.

## In favor
Steve Engel of Precinct 4 called the taking “a bitter pill, a bad option, but it’s the only option to conserve this land.” He said the town is committed to denser development in its center, and Forest Ridge, at the perimeter, offers a natural buffer and a connection to the Fells. He said the connection was a main reason he moved to town. He questioned the $5 million figure, asking whether it describes a fully permitted project, and said the Yellow Book appraisal is a sound basis for a decision.

Diab Jerius of Precinct 8 said the debate comes down to what the town values and what risk it will accept. He said he moved to town in about 1996 and has watched green space become houses, and that his neighborhood is hotter since the trees came down. He called Forest Ridge a special piece of land because it is untrammeled and connected to a larger ecosystem. He questioned the $5 million valuation, saying that if the land can support only one house, it would be strange to value it at that amount. A house with more than one bedroom and a child in the schools is already a net loss in revenue to the town, he said, because one house’s property tax cannot pay for a child’s education. He does not expect development to add real housing diversity, he said, and predicted a series of very large, expensive houses. He said he disagrees with the Housing Partnership Board, which surprised him. He supports more housing, he said, “but we need more housing in appropriate places.”

“I cannot go around my neighborhood and remove the houses and put back the woods that used to be there,” Jerius said. He urged members to vote yes, saying the long-term benefits far outweigh the costs.

## The drinking water question
Caitlin Musto of Precinct 4 noted that backers have cited the drinking water supply and asked whether there is a real risk to it. She also asked whether the town has heard from the state Department of Environmental Protection or the Department of Conservation and Recreation about protecting the land.

DPW Director Robert LaBossiere said the town has received nothing from the Department of Conservation and Recreation, the Environmental Protection Agency or the Department of Environmental Protection about protecting the property. Many houses are closer to the North Reservoir, he said, and the parcel is outside the reservoir’s zone of influence. “We’re not worried about that particular property,” he said, though he added there are always hazards.

updates.title: Finance Committee opposes Forest Ridge taking; Housing Partnership Board urges delay
updates.dek: Community preservation panel offers conditional support; opponents cite financial risk and lawsuits
updates.body:
Boards and committees gave Town Meeting their recommendations on Article 26, and none backed the taking outright.
• Select Board: Split 2-2, with no recommendation.
• Finance Committee: Unfavorable action, with one member dissenting.
• Winchester Committee on Community Preservation: Conditional support for conserving the land, with limits on funding.
• Housing Partnership Board: Voted 7-3 to recommend that Town Meeting delay.

## Select Board
Select Board Chair Anthea Brady said those opposed to a favorable recommendation were concerned primarily about the financial risk and unknowns of a taking by eminent domain.

## Finance Committee
Finance Committee Chair Kathryn Hughes said the Committee voted unfavorable action with one dissenting vote. She said neither the Conservation Commission nor the buyer provided enough information to judge the financial effect of a taking or of development on the town.
• Information the Committee requested and did not receive: the price and terms of the buyer’s purchase agreement, the buyer’s development plans and guarantees of the $1 million federal grant the Commission is counting on.
• The overriding concern: the high probability of one or more lawsuits, Hughes said, with no assessment of that risk. Without the terms of the purchase agreement, she said, there is no way to tell whether Bell Point’s price is higher or lower than the $2.85 million appraisal. She also said it is not clear a taking would qualify the property for the federal grant.

Hughes read from Town Counsel Karis North’s email to interested parties, the same language as the Nov. 3 memo: the town’s offer is “the floor, not the ceiling,” a challenge is “possible and even likely,” and a jury would set the final price.

## Winchester Committee on Community Preservation
Christina Marshall said the Committee did not bring a Forest Ridge borrowing article back because it did not want to repeat the one Town Meeting rejected this spring without changed circumstances. The Committee voted 7-2 to take no action on the borrowing application before it this fall, and 8-1 to issue a statement of conditional support, she said.

She read the Sept. 17 statement. It supports using community preservation money for Forest Ridge, with a permanent conservation restriction, at a price not to exceed the $2.85 million appraisal. The conditions are that Town Meeting votes to take the land and the Select Board votes to carry out the taking. Any money would still need a final application, a Committee vote and an appropriation by Town Meeting. The statement does not allow the Committee to recommend an appropriation, Marshall said.

“We remain supportive of Forest Ridge, but recognize that eminent domain is a significant shift,” she said.

## Housing Partnership Board
John Suhrbier, who was honored earlier in the evening on his retirement from the Board, said it has followed attempts over several years to use the land, including talks with potential developers, and reviewed a memorandum Bell Point LLC submitted at the end of September. He cited three points from the Board’s discussion:
• Bell Point has an agreement to buy the land, so a taking would be from Bell Point rather than the estate.
• Bell Point estimates the land’s value as significantly higher than the Commission assumes.
• Some have said the taking would be unfriendly and likely contested.

Most important to the Board, he said, is that Bell Point’s memorandum offered to work with the town on a combination of conservation and housing that would eliminate the need for eminent domain. He compared that with Wright-Locke Farm, where a small portion used for housing paid for most of the land to be conserved. The Board voted 7-3 to recommend that Town Meeting delay.

updates.title: Olson says taking is ‘only available path’ to save Forest Ridge from development
updates.dek: Commission cites $2.85 million appraisal, 1,300-signature petition and $1.7 million in grants at stake
updates.body:
Conservation Commission Chair Tracy Olson told Town Meeting Monday that an eminent domain taking is “the only available path” to keep Forest Ridge from development. Article 26 would authorize the Select Board to take the 13.7-acre parcel, which abuts the Middlesex Fells, and needs a two-thirds vote.

## The case for conserving it
• The land has three high-quality habitats, assessed by a botanist, with very few non-native plants. The wetlands are part of the town’s drinking water watershed, and the parcel connects the Fells to the Aberjona River as a wildlife corridor.
• The Commission would manage it for walks, birding, school and scout programs. Olson said conservation land raises home values, as at Wright-Locke Farm.

## What has changed since spring
• The developer: Forest Ridge is now under agreement with a developer for housing, Olson said. A 2016 proposal was for a 300-apartment 40B development, and the current developer has suggested the Residential Cluster Development Overlay District, which can allow relatively dense housing.
• The appraisal: A June appraisal put the value at $2.85 million, meeting federal Yellow Book standards.
• The grants: Olson cited a $250,000 earmark from Rep. Michael Day and two state grants totaling about $450,000. She said a federal grant manager told the Commission it is likely to be awarded up to $1 million in early 2027. The state grant can be used in an eminent domain payment, she said, but the federal grant can be used only with the landowner’s agreement.
• The support: More than 1,300 people signed a petition with verified emails. Backers include Friends of the Fells, the Mystic River Watershed Association, Wright-Locke Farm and Friends of Forest Ridge, a new nonprofit of neighbors that would provide stewardship.

## How the process would work
Article 26 is the first step, Olson said. The Commission would then reapply to the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation, which she said supports the funding. Town Meeting would have to approve the borrowing. Last, the Select Board would approve and carry out an order of taking, record it and pay the owner.

The owner would have three years to contest the price and would not get the land back in a challenge, Olson said. She said the developer lacks standing to contest the price unless it has a financial interest in the land, and that the Washington and Swanton streets parcel was taken more than three years ago at its appraised value without a challenge. She called the risk of a challenge low.

Town Counsel Karis North’s Nov. 3 memo says a challenge to the price is “possible and even likely” and that the town’s offer is “the floor, not the ceiling.”

## The money
• Debt service: The $250,000 earmark and the $425,000 state grant total $675,000, about a quarter of the $2.85 million appraisal, leaving a bond of just under $2.2 million. Annual debt service would be about $135,000, which Olson put at 6.6% of fiscal 2027 community preservation revenue, a share she said would shrink over time. With the federal grant, she said, grants would cover half the value, about $1.425 million, and the cost would drop to $85,000. By Olson’s own account, that scenario depends on the owner’s agreement.
• Operating costs and taxes: Trails to the Fells and a small parking lot off Forest Circle would be built with volunteers, scouts and grants, Olson said, so there would be no new operating cost and no tax increase. The land now yields about $54,000 a year in property tax, against fiscal 2026 town revenue of $172 million.
• Development costs: She said reviews of earlier proposals documented water, sewer and stormwater upgrades and new students, at about $19,000 per pupil, which she said equals the tax from a $1.7 million home.

## Why now
Olson said the parcel probably has more than 1,800 trees, which would cost well over $1 million to replace. She contrasted that with the 50-tree project Town Meeting approved earlier. Waiting risks up to $1.7 million in grants and earmarks, she said, and borrowing costs are low but rising. If the developer proceeds, she said, the land’s value will rise and could put it out of reach.

Olson called the property “a lasting gift to our community, especially our children.”

## Where this differs from earlier reporting
• The petition: Olson cited more than 1,300 signatures. The Commission’s handout said almost 600.
• The federal grant: The $85,000 scenario depends on the owner’s agreement, which Olson acknowledged. Winchester News has reported the grant is not in hand.

Town Meeting took up Article 26 Monday, the Conservation Commission’s proposal to take the Forest Ridge parcel off Forest Circle by eminent domain. Commission Chair Tracy Olson is presenting the case. The article needs a two-thirds vote. The Select Board deadlocked 2-2 earlier in the evening on a motion to recommend favorable action.

[[inline:1]]
A slide titled “Debt service estimates are lower than Spring TM” showed two scenarios:
• With a state grant: A $2,175,000 bond, after a $425,000 state Local Acquisitions for Natural Diversity grant and a $250,000 legislative earmark, would cost an estimated $135,000 a year in debt service from community preservation money, or 6.6% of fiscal 2027 community preservation revenue, according to the slide.
• With state and federal grants: A $1,425,000 bond, after the $425,000 state grant and a $1 million federal Land and Water Conservation Fund grant, would cost an estimated $85,000 a year, or 4.1% of that revenue.

Winchester News has reported that the federal grant is not in hand, and that federal rules allow it in an eminent domain taking only with the owner’s agreement. updates.title: Town Meeting approves community preservation projects, rejects Nutile Field master plan
updates.dek: Clicker vote of 65-93 sinks $50,000 request as members question process
updates.body:
Town Meeting approved seven of the eight projects in Article 25 Monday and rejected a $50,000 master plan for Nutile Field. The Nutile motion failed on a clicker vote, 65 yes, 93 no and two abstentions, though the Select Board recommended favorable action. Members took each motion separately.

[[inline:1]]

## The results
• Motion 1, Leonard Field pavilion, $300,000: passed unanimously on a voice vote.
• Motion 2, Lincoln School shade, $35,000: passed unanimously.
• Motion 3, McDonald Field tennis courts, $35,000: passed unanimously.
• Motion 4, Nutile Field master plan, $50,000: failed, 65-93 with two abstentions. It needed a majority.
• Motion 5, Packer-Ellis courts, $400,000: passed on a voice vote.
• Motion 6, park tree canopy, $60,000: passed on a voice vote.
• Motion 7, Town Hall auditorium seating, $25,000: passed on a voice vote.
• Motion 8, Tri-Community Greenway, $15,500: passed unanimously.

The approved motions total $870,500 of the $920,500 proposed.

## The Nutile Field debate
• In favor: Michael Bettencourt of Precinct 6 said the community preservation fund holds about $1.8 million. He said the field master plan work that began around 2017 was always meant to be phased in, and that the youth baseball program has largely maintained Nutile with little town money.
• Against: Diab Jerius of Precinct 8 said he is torn but wants a strategic look at all fields first. “I am going to vote against that motion, just so that we have a chance in the future to use the word strategic again,” he said. Marilyn Gagalis of Precinct 1 said there should be one master plan for all town-owned fields. Michael Creane of Precinct 8, who chairs the Fields Management Committee and coaches in the Nutile program, said the program deserves support but that the proponents did not coordinate with related committees, as the guidelines for applications to the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation ask.

## Other questions
• Forest Ridge: Andy Mills, a new member from Precinct 5, asked about the “nearly $3 million” of borrowing mentioned during the presentation. Christina Marshall said the slide showed an application to acquire the Forest Ridge parcel that the Committee did not advance to Town Meeting. All eight motions use cash on hand, she said.
• Who runs the work: Christian Nixon of Precinct 1 asked who will manage procurement and whether managers have the capacity. Marshall said the entities in charge of the town-owned sites signed off, and the Town Manager’s Office met with proponents and agreed they can do the work.
• Leonard Field restrooms: Roger Wilson Jr. of Precinct 1 asked whether Motion 1 means portable toilets with a roof. Marshall said yes, that is the current plan. He asked that the final plans account for heavy service trucks, which now cross the bike path and grass. A Winchester Recreation official said permanent restrooms were dropped because of cost. The original master plan, with a pavilion and restrooms, would have topped half a million dollars.
• Packer-Ellis: Susan DeLeo of Precinct 5 suggested raising out-of-town membership fees. The official said Winchester Recreation reviews fees every year and raises them routinely. Pamela Cort of Precinct 5 spoke in favor, praising the recreation director’s work.

updates.body:
Town Meeting is debating Article 25, the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation’s $920,500 package of eight projects, and has not yet voted on any of them. A 4th grader asking for shade at her school and three Winchester High School tennis captains asking for court funding spoke in favor. Members questioned the Packer-Ellis tennis courts project and a master plan for Nutile Field.

[[inline:1]]

## The eight projects
• Motion 1, Leonard Field pavilion: $300,000 to remove the former bathhouse and build a community pavilion and restrooms, the last phase of the Leonard Field revitalization.
• Motion 2, Lincoln School shade: $35,000 for two shade structures covering about 512 square feet.
• Motion 3, McDonald Field tennis courts: $35,000 to resurface the courts. Christina Marshall, who presented the Committee’s report, said the Committee weighed full reconstruction and decided resurfacing was the better financial choice.
• Motion 4, Nutile Field master plan: $50,000.
• Motion 5, Packer-Ellis courts: $400,000 for final design, permitting and construction-ready plans.
• Motion 6, park tree canopy: $60,000 to plant up to 50 trees at Davidson Park, Elliot Park, Ginn Field and McDonald Field.
• Motion 7, Town Hall auditorium seating: $25,000 to restore the balcony seating.
• Motion 8, Tri-Community Greenway: $15,500 for six small safety and comfort improvements.

## The Committee’s report
Marshall presented the Committee’s report.
• The process: The Committee received 13 initial applications and nine final ones, and advanced eight to Town Meeting. Marshall said the Leonard Field pavilion, McDonald Field courts and Packer-Ellis courts were also submitted to the Capital Planning Committee, and the Committee agreed to fund all three in full.
• The money: The Committee estimates it will have just under $4 million in the bank for fiscal 2028, counting about $750,000 from fiscal 2026, just over $1 million unspent from fiscal 2027 if all eight motions pass and about $2 million expected in fiscal 2028.
• Recommendations: Marshall said the Select Board voted favorable action on all eight motions. School Committee Chair Timothy Matthews said the School Committee took up only Motions 2 and 8, the shade structures and the greenway, and voted unanimous favorable action on both.

“We cannot fund what we are not asked to fund,” Marshall said, urging anyone with an eligible project to apply.

## Lincoln School shade (Motion 2)
Marshall said the project grew out of a school newspaper article by Lucy Gray, a 4th grader at Lincoln Elementary. The Lincoln School Parents Association saw it and reached out to the School Committee. With Town Meeting’s consent, Lucy spoke.

She told members she wrote the article last spring about the need for “more shade outside to enjoy recess,” interviewed many other students who agreed, and made the paper’s front page. “I am here tonight to support this motion,” she said.

A member asked whether trees could also be planted at the Lincoln playground. Marshall said that is not part of the motion but is an option for the future.

## Packer-Ellis courts (Motion 5)
[[inline:2]]
Marshall said the courts are more than 103 years old and among the largest municipal clay-court facilities in the United States. Earlier community preservation money paid for the first two phases, a concept plan and engineering. This phase would produce a permitted, bid-ready plan, with the work running through fall 2028. Marshall said the project should return to the Committee and to the Capital Planning Committee for construction money.

Three Winchester High School tennis captains urged members to support it:
• Evan Ware, captain of the boys team, said the team moves to the clay courts for the second half of its season. “We’re the only high school team in the state that gets to play on clay,” he said.
• Isha Bala, a senior and captain of the girls varsity team, said she started playing at 5 in Winchester Recreation summer clinics and later coached younger children on the same courts.
• Olivia Thompson, a senior and co-captain of the girls team, said the courts are home to both state championship-winning high school teams. “I have made so many amazing memories and a lot of mistakes on these courts,” she said.

Brenda Mandile of Precinct 6 asked how much the first two phases cost, what the full project would cost and whether private money had been promised. A Winchester Recreation official said the first phase was a $60,000 concept plan raised a few years ago and the second covered structural engineering for failing retaining walls and stormwater work. The site is in a flood zone and needs a full site plan review, the official said. Winchester Recreation does not plan to ask for the full cost, the official said, and is pursuing a U.S. Tennis Association grant capped at $150,000, state grants including a Land and Water Conservation Fund grant, capital funding and recreation retained earnings, and possibly water and sewer retained earnings. A nonprofit tennis association has started talking about fundraising, which the official said is a couple of years away.

## Nutile Field master plan (Motion 4)
Marshall said Winchester Recreation, the youth softball and baseball groups and the Town Manager’s Office asked for the $50,000. The field serves hundreds of children a year, and its needs include replacing aging fencing, backstops and dugouts and improving parking.

Robin Vos of Precinct 3 said she opposes Motion 4, not because the field is unworthy but because of process. The Committee is new, she said, and Town Meeting can help shape it with its votes. She asked for the kind of collaboration it has with the Capital Planning Committee and for an update from the Fields Management Committee.

Its chair, Michael Creane, said the Fields Management Committee, Winchester Recreation and the Town Manager’s Office are talking about revisiting the roughly 10-year-old field management master plan to look at every field. He said he personally thinks a full town master plan matters more than many individual field plans.

## Another question
A member asked whether the Leonard Field restrooms would use composting toilets instead of full plumbing. Marshall said the restroom picture shown was a mockup and final decisions have not been made.

updates.title: Town Meeting approves police superiors contract, budget director post unanimously
updates.dek: Package adds top pay step and restores longevity pay; two transfers total $191,000
updates.body:
Town Meeting approved Article 24 unanimously Monday, a package of four Personnel Board motions that ratifies a new contract for police superiors and creates a budget director position. Moderator Philip Frattaroli grouped the motions into one voice vote. Peter Cheimets of Precinct 5 presented the article. He said the Select Board and the Finance Committee each voted favorable action on all four motions. The Select Board had taken no vote on the article Nov. 2. Cheimets said one more contract is still unsettled.

## What the motions do
• The contract: Police superiors get raises of 2.5% retroactive for fiscal 2026, 2.5% for fiscal 2027 and 1% for fiscal 2028, each measured against base pay. The materials did not include the superiors’ base payroll needed to turn the 2.5% raises into dollars. A new step at the top of the pay range, worth 4%, begins in fiscal 2028, which is why that year’s raise is smaller. Many superior officers are at the top of the range now, Cheimets said, so the step gives them room to move up. In fiscal 2028, about $40,000 of the cost is the 1% raise and $84,000 is the new step, which keeps the total close to where a 2.5% raise would have put it.
• Stipends: The defensive tactics and Taser training officer and the technology officer each get 2% more. The materials did not include their base pay needed to turn that into dollars. A police trainer for standards and training gets $500 in fiscal 2026 and $1,000 in fiscal 2027.
• Longevity pay: The contract changes longevity pay for police superiors for the first time in eight years, Cheimets said. The last change was in 2017. The amounts will be set yearly through the contract.
• $60,500 from free cash goes into the fiscal 2027 personal services budget to cover the retroactive pay.
• $130,500 moves from the unallocated wage budget into the police personal services budget for fiscal 2027.
• The budget director: The fourth motion creates the position but does not fund it. Cheimets said that is a separate process.

## Why the money is split this way
The contract is being settled partway through the year. The town has to pay all of fiscal 2026 and about half of fiscal 2027 retroactively, Cheimets said, and cover higher costs for the rest of fiscal 2027. Fiscal 2028 will be handled in that year’s appropriation. He said the unallocated wage budget exists for this purpose: the town sets money aside for contracts that are unsettled when the year begins, so the cost does not hit all at once when they are settled years later.

“Of course all of you are jumping to the question of why 1% in FY 28, which was where I went immediately,” Cheimets said.

updates.body:
Town Meeting approved Article 19 unanimously Monday after cutting the transfer to the town’s retiree health trust from $350,000 to $175,000. Members carried Select Board member Michelle Prior’s amendment on a clicker vote and passed the amended motion by voice vote. The money comes from free cash and goes to the town’s other post-employment benefits trust. Moderator Philip Frattaroli took up the article first.

## The presentation
Select Board Chair Anthea Brady presented the article.
• The trust holds about $9.8 million against a total OPEB liability of about $119.7 million, leaving about $109.8 million unfunded. The funded share, trust assets as a portion of the total liability, rose to 8.22%, or about $9.8 million of the $119.7 million, from 5.93% last year. The materials did not include last year’s liability needed to turn the 5.93% into dollars.
• A change in retiree health benefit provisions cut the calculated liability by about $22.3 million. Brady said the drop came mainly from benefit and actuarial changes, not added contributions.
• The fiscal 2026 actuarial report assumes the town contributes $350,000 a year beyond its pay-as-you-go costs until the pension system is fully funded, which she said should happen within a year or two. Pension money would then shift to OPEB.
• The Select Board split 2-2 on a recommendation.

Finance Committee Chair Kathryn Hughes said the Committee voted favorable action on the full $350,000, with one member opposed. She said the Committee treats the payment as a fixed expense that belongs in the annual budget, and that it agreed to leave the money out of the spring budget to hold down free cash use. With interest income up, she said, the money is there. Hughes called the vote a sympathetic one, saying members kept hearing that retirees worked hard for the town and are owed this.

## The amendment
Prior, who had asked that the article come off the consent agenda, said she is one of the two Select Board members who voted against the full amount. She served on the Finance Committee when the town made its first $50,000 contribution, she said, noting the trust had no money in 2012 and holds $9.8 million today.

The town could spend $1.3 million in free cash before spring, she said, before it knows what fiscal 2028 looks like. “We are reducing the flexibility to fund next year’s budget by taking out free cash in this and other articles,” Prior said. She said she asked Town Manager Christopher Senior at a pre-meeting Monday for options to fund the other half in the spring by repurposing funds, closing accounts or adjusting budgets.

Brady said the Board stayed split on the amendment: members opposed favor $350,000 as written, and those in favor support half. The Finance Committee backed the amendment 9-3.

## Questions from the floor
• Pensions: Brian McCarthy of Precinct 4 asked whether the actuarial assumptions count pension money flowing into OPEB. Brady said they do, and answered yes when he asked whether all of the money now going to the pension would move to OPEB once it is paid off.
• Why now: Another member asked why the money goes in now instead of in the spring, and what waiting would cost. A town official said it matters little when the money goes in; the difference is where it comes from. The official said the interest impact would be negligible. The town put nothing in at spring Town Meeting, the official said, because the payment was taken out of the fiscal 2027 budget to balance it, so tonight is a catch-up.

## The votes
• Amendment to reduce the transfer from $350,000 to $175,000: carried on a clicker vote, 98 to 46.
• Main motion as amended, to transfer $175,000 from free cash to the OPEB trust to reduce the unfunded liability: carried unanimously by voice vote.

updates.title: Select Board deadlocks on Forest Ridge, retiree health; backs Committee on Names
updates.dek: Tie leaves eminent domain article without favorable recommendation as town counsel memo outlines two-step process

images.caption: A Conservation Commission handout on Article 26 circulates before Town Meeting’s second session Monday.
images.credit: WINCHESTER NEWS STAFF PHOTO / WILL DOWD

updates.body:
The Select Board deadlocked 2-2 Monday on a motion to recommend favorable action on Article 26, the proposed eminent domain taking of Forest Ridge, and the motion failed to obtain the majority it needed. Members also voted 3-1 to recommend favorable action on Article 38, which would make the Committee on Names a standing Town Meeting committee, and deadlocked 2-2 on a motion for favorable action on Article 19, a $350,000 free cash transfer to the town’s retiree health trust. Both tied motions failed to obtain a majority. Members met in the principal’s office at Winchester High School before Town Meeting’s second session.

## Forest Ridge: how members voted
• Michael Bettencourt: yes
• Michelle Prior: yes
• Bill McGonigle: no
• Anthea Brady: no

Bettencourt is a co-sponsor of the article with the Conservation Commission. The Board’s recommendation is advisory. It put off the question Nov. 2 without a vote. Town Meeting needs a two-thirds vote to authorize a taking, and Town Counsel Karis North wrote in a Nov. 3 memo that the Select Board would then have to vote separately, by majority, to carry it out. In May, Town Meeting rejected a voluntary $3 million purchase of the land, 105-59.

[[documents]]

## What North’s memo means for Article 26
North’s Nov. 3 memo to Town Meeting is a general overview of eminent domain. It does not mention Forest Ridge, its appraisals or its financing. Here is how it applies to Article 26.
• Two approvals are needed. A taking requires a two-thirds Town Meeting vote and a majority of the Select Board. The Board’s recommendation Monday is advisory. The vote that counts is the Board’s separate decision to carry out a taking. A tied Board would not have the majority the memo requires.
• Town Meeting cannot compel it. The memo says a Town Meeting vote can authorize a taking but cannot direct the Board to make one, even when the Conservation Commission starts the process.
• The town’s offer is not the final price. The owner has three years to sue over the amount, and a jury sets fair market value. The memo says the offer “is the floor, not the ceiling,” and that a challenge is “possible and even likely.” The town would pay any increase plus statutory interest. In the memo’s example, a $10 million offer and a $15 million verdict mean $5 million more.
• It can’t be undone. The town owns the land once the order of taking is recorded, even if the price is disputed. Each side pays its own legal fees, and the memo says most cases reach trial about three years after filing.
• Purpose can be challenged. The taking must serve a public purpose, and the memo says a court that finds none could return the land.

Winchester News has reported that a reliable net cost to the town cannot be calculated from the public record. The memo suggests any estimate built on the town’s offer is a minimum.

The handout’s statement that fair market value is “legally guaranteed” and the memo’s description fit together. The owner is entitled to fair market value, but the amount may not be known until a jury decides.

## The Conservation Commission’s handout
A one-page handout from the Commission makes the case for Article 26. It describes Forest Ridge as a 13.7-acre privately owned parcel abutting the Middlesex Fells and says taking it would protect wetlands, the North Reservoir watershed and wildlife habitat.
• Support: The handout says almost 600 people signed a petition to acquire the land for conservation.
• Why eminent domain: It says the land is under agreement with a developer who is working to buy a house lot on Forest Circle to improve access, so the town cannot buy it directly.
• Money: It lists a $250,000 state earmark, a $425,000 state grant it says has been awarded and a $1 million federal grant it calls likely. It says annual debt service would take no more than 4% to 7% of the Winchester Committee on Community Preservation’s projected $2 million in fiscal 2027 revenue, or $80,000 to $140,000 a year.
• After a taking: The Commission would oversee the land for passive recreation and arrange trails connecting entrances to the Fells. The handout says improvements would use grants or volunteer labor and no town funds would be requested.

“Forest Ridge is a smart acquisition and a lasting gift to our community, especially our children,” the handout concludes.

## Where earlier reporting differs
• Assessed value: The handout calls $2.85 million the assessed value. That figure is from a June appraisal, and the town assesses the parcels at about $4.9 million.
• Federal grant: The handout calls it likely. It is not in hand, and federal rules allow it in an eminent domain taking only with the owner’s agreement.

## Article 38: Committee on Names
Prior made the motion, and Brady voted yes. McGonigle voted no.
• School property: Members asked whether leaving out explicit language that schools keep authority over their own property could confuse readers or weaken other boards’ authority. An official said the Committee’s role is advisory and cannot override state law. Prior said North, asked about it, saw no concern.
• The moderator: McGonigle, who voted no, said he did not think the language had to be added back, but that a stronger introduction stressing the Committee’s advisory role would help readers. He said he thinks the moderator should stay neutral and not be a voting member. Prior said the Committee on Names met last week, discussed the question and voted to keep the moderator provision as written, with the moderator able to break ties.

## Article 19: Retiree health transfer
The Board deadlocked 2-2 on a motion for favorable action, and the motion failed to obtain a majority, according to a town official. The Board took no vote Nov. 2, when a motion for a favorable recommendation died for lack of a second. Moderator Philip Frattaroli pulled the article from the consent agenda Thursday. Prior had argued for splitting the contribution between the fall and spring meetings.

updates.title: Town Meeting returns tonight with Forest Ridge taking still ahead
updates.dek: Members face 19 remaining articles, from a $400,000 school reserve to five citizen petitions
updates.body:
Town Meeting resumes at 7 p.m. at Winchester High School for its second session. Members acted on 26 of the 45 articles Thursday, leaving 19, including the warrant’s most contested questions. Thursday, Nov. 12, is also scheduled, and Nov. 16 is held in reserve.

## What to watch
• Forest Ridge (Article 26): The Conservation Commission wants authority to take about 13.4 acres off Forest Circle by eminent domain, which needs a two-thirds vote. A June appraisal valued the land at $2.85 million. In May, Town Meeting rejected a voluntary $3 million purchase, 105-59. Select Board Chair Anthea Brady has said she expects the article on the second or third night.
• Retiree health (Article 19): The moderator pulled this $350,000 free cash transfer to the retiree health trust from the consent agenda Thursday. The Select Board took no position Nov. 2, when a motion for a favorable recommendation died for lack of a second.
• Special education reserve (Article 29): The schools want $400,000. The Select Board backed it 3-1; member Michelle Prior voted no, saying she favored $200,000.
• Sanborn Carriage House (Article 30): A $50,000 study of refurbishing, replacing or demolishing the building. The Select Board voted 4-0 against it, the only article the Board opposes.
• Software (Article 33): Two motions totaling $331,465.68 for permitting and budget software. The Select Board deferred it Nov. 2 amid disagreement over using about $92,000 in free cash.
• Community preservation (Article 25): $920,500 for eight projects, including $400,000 to prepare the Packer-Ellis tennis courts for bidding and $300,000 for the Leonard pavilion.

## Also on the warrant
• Article 24: Police superiors’ pay and a new budget director position.
• Articles 34 through 38: Tougher sidewalk snow-clearing rules; three land items tied to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority station, the Waterfield project and about 16 acres under the Montvale Land settlement; and a standing Committee on Names.
• Articles 39 through 43, citizen petitions: Rezonings at 114 Church St. and 18 Raymond Place, two Ledges articles for one new house lot and a call for separate override votes. The Church Street petitioner’s attorney told the Select Board Nov. 2 that the petitioner would not pursue it this fall.
• Articles 44 and 45: A fiscal 2027 tax levy reduction and committee housekeeping. No motion had been printed for either.

## What a Forest Ridge vote would do
Town Counsel Karis North’s Nov. 3 memo to Town Meeting lays out the steps:
• A two-thirds Town Meeting vote only authorizes a taking. The Select Board then decides by majority vote whether to carry it out, and no taking can happen without both.
• Once the Select Board records an order of taking, the town owns the land and must offer compensation within 30 days.
• The owner has three years to sue over the price, and a jury sets fair market value. The town would pay any difference plus statutory interest, and the taking cannot be undone.

The town’s offer “is the floor, not the ceiling,” North wrote, adding that a challenge to the valuation is “possible and even likely.”

Night one’s summary, full video and coverage follow tonight’s posts.
